AI.result: Proton temperatures exceed 2 MK at Parker; speed at ~10 R_sun is only ~60% of its asymptotic value; acceleration is largely complete by 60 R_sun; fluctuations evolve from near-transverse small-angle at Parker to full reversal switchbacks at Solar Orbiter; the low coronal acceleration resembles polar coronal hole flows; observed thermal pressure gradients are insufficient to drive the acceleration, requiring energy from Alfvénic fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The multi-spacecraft observations provide unique constraints on models of the radial evolution of the fastest solar wind, indicating gradual, steady acceleration over the first few tens of solar radii, with Alfvénic fluctuation energy playing a significant role in the acceleration process.

title: Extragalactic Stellar Streams in Time-Dependent Cosmological Halos
comment: Submitted to ApJ, 34 pages, 22 figures
summary: Upcoming and ongoing surveys will detect thousands of stellar streams around galaxies other than the Milky Way. Studies from the Milky Way have shown that time-dependent evolution of the Galactic halo plays a key role in shaping stellar streams, but remains unexplored for extragalactic stellar streams. We use the FIRE-2 m12m cosmological zoom-in simulation, mock observed as an extragalactic system including three stellar streams, to examine how halo time-dependence affects progenitor and host halo inference from extragalactic systems. We show that two of the three m12m streams are well reproduced in a static halo if we only allow for tidal stripping near pericenter. We apply the extragalactic stream fitting code X-Stream to each mock observed stream, and obtain constraints on the host dark matter halo and stream properties. Using on-sky morphology alone and then fixing the progenitor radial velocities, we compare recovered orbits and halo parameters to the FIRE-2 m12m ground truth. For the longest stream with a looped segment, we find unbiased strong constraints on progenitor and halo properties. For the shortest stream, we find limits on orbital parameters, but no constraints on progenitor and halo mass unless we include fainter, more extended debris. For the most massive stream, which was not well produced in a static halo, the recovered orbital parameters are biased, reflecting unmodeled time-dependence. We conclude that imaging of stream debris from extragalactic dwarf galaxies can, in some cases, be used to infer present-day dark matter halo properties, even in a cosmological environment.

AI.tldr: Using the FIRE-2 m12m cosmological zoom-in simulation with three mock-observed extragalactic stellar streams, the authors test whether static-halo stream models can recover correct host halo and progenitor properties. They find that two of three streams are well-reproduced in a static halo (with tidal stripping near pericenter), yielding unbiased constraints for the longest stream and limited constraints for the shortest, while the most massive stream produces biased orbital parameters due to unmodeled time-dependent halo evolution.
AI.motivation: Upcoming surveys will detect thousands of extragalactic stellar streams. While time-dependent Galactic halo evolution is known to shape Milky Way streams, this effect remains unexplored for extragalactic streams, raising the question of whether static-halo inference tools are valid in cosmological environments.
AI.method: The work uses the FIRE-2 m12m cosmological zoom-in simulation, mock observed as an extragalactic system containing three stellar streams. The authors test static-halo reproduction with tidal stripping near pericenter, then apply the extragalactic stream fitting code X-Stream to each mock stream, using on-sky morphology and fixed progenitor radial velocities to recover orbital and halo parameters, compared against the FIRE-2 ground truth.
AI.result: Two of three streams are well reproduced in a static halo with pericenter tidal stripping. The longest stream (with a looped segment) yields unbiased strong constraints on progenitor and halo properties. The shortest stream yields only orbital parameter limits with no mass constraints unless fainter, more extended debris is included. The most massive stream, poorly reproduced in a static halo, gives biased orbital parameters due to unmodeled time-dependence.
AI.conclusion: Imaging of extragalactic dwarf galaxy stream debris can, in some cases, successfully infer present-day dark matter halo properties even in a cosmological (time-dependent) environment.

title: The Formation of Very Close Binary Stars
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The majority of very close binaries (orbital periods P < 5 days) are in triples. Previous studies surmised that the tertiary hardened the inner binary via Kozai-Lidov cycles coupled with tidal friction. Alternatively, the trend could be due to a common origin, e.g., more massive molecular cores and protostellar disks are more likely to fragment twice into a triple and harden the inner binary to very short periods via disk migration. Disk migration occurs during the embedded Class I protostellar phase while secular evolution with a tertiary occurs on much longer timescales. To determine the dominant migration mechanism, I accurately measure the very close binary fractions of both late-type and early-type primaries in star-forming environments. After combining five surveys, the late-type Class II/III T Tauri very close binary fraction is F_VCB = 2.1_{-0.5}^{+1.0}%, which is consistent with the measurement for late-type field main-sequence stars (1.7% +/- 0.1%). More than 85% of very close late-type binaries hardened via disk migration during the Class I protostellar phase. I next measure the OGLE-III eclipsing binary (EB) fractions of young massive stars in the LMC. The very close EB fractions of massive young stellar objects (YSOs; F_VCEB = 8.3_{-3.2}^{+4.9}%), OB stars near massive YSOs (4.7% +/- 0.8%), and OB stars in small, young H II regions (6.4% +/- 1.5%) are consistent with each other and the measurement for OB stars in slightly older clusters (4.7% +/- 0.3%). More than 90% of very close massive binaries hardened via disk migration during the embedded protostellar phase.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the dominant formation mechanism for very close binaries (P < 5 days), which are predominantly found in triples. By measuring very close binary fractions across late-type T Tauri stars and early-type massive stars in star-forming regions and comparing them to field populations, the author concludes that disk migration during the embedded Class I protostellar phase (rather than Kozai-Lidov cycles with a tertiary) is the dominant hardening mechanism for more than 85% of very close late-type binaries and more than 90% of very close massive binaries.
AI.motivation: Very close binaries (P < 5 days) are overwhelmingly found in triple systems, raising the question of whether the tertiary dynamically hardens the inner binary via Kozai-Lidov cycles with tidal friction, or whether a common origin (fragmentation into triples plus disk migration) explains the trend. Distinguishing these mechanisms requires measuring close binary fractions in young star-forming environments, where disk migration (during the Class I phase) and secular tertiary evolution operate on very different timescales.
AI.method: The author combines five surveys to measure the very close binary fraction of late-type Class II/III T Tauri stars in star-forming regions, and uses OGLE-III eclipsing binary data to measure very close eclipsing binary fractions of massive young stellar objects, OB stars near massive YSOs, and OB stars in small young H II regions in the LMC. These young populations are then compared to field main-sequence binaries to determine which hardening mechanism dominates.
AI.result: The late-type Class II/III T Tauri very close binary fraction is F_VCB = 2.1_{-0.5}^{+1.0}%, consistent with the field late-type fraction (1.7% +/- 0.1%). For massive stars, the very close eclipsing binary fractions of massive YSOs (8.3%), OB stars near massive YSOs (4.7%), and OB stars in small young H II regions (6.4%) are all consistent with each other and with slightly older cluster OB stars (4.7%).
AI.conclusion: Since very close binary fractions in the youngest populations already match field values (implying they form early), and disk migration operates during the short-lived embedded Class I phase while Kozai-Lidov secular evolution takes much longer, the author concludes that disk migration is the dominant mechanism. This accounts for more than 85% of very close late-type binaries and more than 90% of very close massive binaries, ruling out tertiary-driven Kozai-Lidov hardening as the primary channel.

title: The Stellar Populations of Two Quiescent Low Surface Brightness Dwarf Galaxies in Low Density Environments
comment: 12 pages, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Dwarf galaxies located in low density environments that have quiescent stellar populations are extremely rare and the mechanism for quenching their stars is highly uncertain. Here we present two low surface brightness dwarf galaxies with large (>1.2 kpc) effective radii that were previously identified in the Dragonfly Ultrawide Survey for which we have obtained spectra using the KCWI instrument on the Keck II telescope. We derive their stellar populations and star formation histories in several radial bins out to 1.25 effective radii. Globally both galaxies are old (~9 Gyr) and metal-poor ([M/H] ~ -1) and reveal quenching on a relatively rapid timescale (~1 Gyr). We find flat to rising age and metallicity gradients in both galaxies. This is similar to those seen in ultra diffuse galaxies but is in contrast with typical classical dwarf galaxies and predictions from simulations. One galaxy, DFUWS 68, hosts several globular clusters which we find to share similar ages, metallicities and quenching timescales to that of the host galaxy stars.We briefly discuss possible quenching mechanisms and suggest that neither cosmic web stripping nor internal feedback processes alone can explain our results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents KCWI spectroscopy of two rare quiescent low surface brightness dwarf galaxies with large effective radii (>1.2 kpc) from the Dragonfly Ultrawide Survey, revealing old (~9 Gyr), metal-poor ([M/H] ~ -1) stellar populations that quenched rapidly (~1 Gyr), with flat/rising age and metallicity gradients similar to ultra diffuse galaxies but contrasting classical dwarfs and simulations.
AI.motivation: Quiescent dwarf galaxies in low-density environments are extremely rare, and the mechanisms that quench their star formation are highly uncertain. Understanding these objects can provide insights into dwarf galaxy evolution and the processes that shut down star formation outside of dense cluster environments.
AI.method: The authors obtained rest-frame optical spectra using the KCWI instrument on the Keck II telescope for two low surface brightness dwarf galaxies with large effective radii, previously identified in the Dragonfly Ultrawide Survey. They derived stellar populations and star formation histories in multiple radial bins out to 1.25 effective radii.
AI.result: Both galaxies are globally old (~9 Gyr) and metal-poor ([M/H] ~ -1), with fast quenching timescales (~1 Gyr). They exhibit flat to rising age and metallicity gradients, similar to ultra diffuse galaxies but opposite to classical dwarf galaxies and simulation predictions. One galaxy (DFUWS 68) hosts globular clusters sharing similar ages, metallicities, and quenching timescales with the host galaxy.
AI.conclusion: Neither cosmic web stripping nor internal feedback processes alone can explain the observed properties, suggesting more complex or alternative quenching mechanisms may be required for these rare objects.

title: Age Discrepancy in Three Galactic Cepheid Binaries
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: SV Per, RW Cam, and KN Cen are Galactic classical Cepheids found in binary systems along with B-type companions. Each system exhibits an ``apparent age discrepancy", where the Cepheid appears significantly younger than its companion. We compute stellar evolution tracks using the MESA code and compare them with these stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram to estimate the masses and the corresponding ages. We find that, for two of the systems, the companions appear to be between 1.5 times to double the age of the Cepheids, suggesting that the Cepheids may be rejuvenated merger products of two main-sequence stars that have since evolved. We find that the third system KN Cen is consistent with single star evolution when we reevaluate ultraviolet observations and find that the companion is hotter than previously measured. We test this idea using the MESA code for each system by evolving a single star model and rapidly accreting mass on the main sequence to emulate a merger, and then continuing the evolution until the model is consistent with the parameters of the Cepheids. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that the Cepheids were originally merger products. We conclude with a discussion of potential observational tests of the merger hypothesis.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates three Galactic classical Cepheids (SV Per, RW Cam, KN Cen) in binary systems with B-type companions that show an apparent age discrepancy. Using MESA stellar evolution models, the authors find that for SV Per and RW Cam the companions appear 1.5-2x older than the Cepheids, suggesting these Cepheids are rejuvenated merger products. However, KN Cen is found consistent with single-star evolution after re-evaluating ultraviolet observations with a hotter companion than previously thought. Merger simulations via rapid mass accretion reproduce the Cepheid parameters, confirming the merger hypothesis for two systems.
AI.motivation: To resolve the "apparent age discrepancy" in three binary systems where the Cepheid appears significantly younger than its B-type companion, potentially indicating that some Cepheids are not products of standard single-star evolution but rather rejuvenated merger products of main-sequence stars.
AI.method: The authors compute stellar evolution tracks with the MESA code and compare them with observed stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram to estimate masses and ages. They also re-evaluate ultraviolet observations for KN Cen. To test the merger hypothesis, they evolve single-star models with rapid mass accretion on the main sequence (emulating a merger) and continue evolution until consistency with observed Cepheid parameters is achieved.
AI.result: For SV Per and RW Cam, companions are found to be 1.5-2 times older than the Cepheids, supporting a merger origin for the Cepheids. For KN Cen, re-analysis of UV data reveals a hotter companion than previously measured, making it consistent with single-star evolution. Merging emulation models successfully reproduced the observed Cepheid parameters for the two candidate systems.
AI.conclusion: The results support the hypothesis that at least two of the Cepheids (SV Per and RW Cam) were originally merger products, while KN Cen is consistent with single-star evolution. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential observational tests for the merger hypothesis.

title: H II region filling factors in NGC 628: Luminosity-size relation and connection with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission
comment: 29 pages, 24 figures, Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Understanding the internal structure of H II regions is fundamental for constraining star formation processes in galaxies. We investigated how the filling factor (FF) relates to luminosity, size, electron density, and H$α$ equivalent width (EW(H$α$)) in H II regions, and explored its connection with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-to-dust emission as a possible tracer of evolutionary stages. We analyzed 622 H II regions in NGC~628, combining 475 regions from SIGNALS and 147 from PHANGS-MUSE. We derived their luminosities, emission-line fluxes, radii, electron densities, and FF, and used PHANGS-JWST/MIRI imaging to quantify the PAH-to-dust ratio $R_{\rm PAH}$ from the 7.7, 11.3, and 21~$μ$m bands. Higher FF and EW(H$α$) values are found in luminous regions, whereas more extended regions with lower EW(H$α$) exhibit lower FF. We show that the H II region radius definition significantly affects the $L_{\rm Hα}$--$R$ relation. Low-luminosity compact H II regions appear to mark a transition from cluster-powered regions to nebulae ionized by single massive stars, around $\log(L_{\rm Hα}) \sim 37~{\rm erg \ s^{-1}}$. The PAH-to-dust ratio correlates with the volumetric H$α$ luminosity density, $L_{\rm Hα}/R^3$, with a transition around $\log(L_{\rm Hα}/R^3) \sim 32~{\rm erg \ s^{-1}}$, corresponding to $\log({\rm FF}) \approx -4.4$. Regions with lower FF exhibit higher $R_{\rm PAH}$, suggesting less efficient PAH processing in more porous structures. These results are consistent with an evolutionary scenario in which FF decreases with stellar cluster age as giant H II regions evolve toward fainter and more extended states. The volumetric H$α$ luminosity density reduces covariance between $L_{\rm Hα}$ and $R$ induced by region-definition methods, enabling more consistent cross-catalog comparisons.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 622 H II regions in NGC 628 (from SIGNALS and PHANGS-MUSE) to investigate how the filling factor (FF) relates to luminosity, size, electron density, and Hα equivalent width, and how these correlate with the PAH-to-dust ratio as an evolutionary tracer. Higher FF and EW(Hα) are found in luminous regions, while larger, fainter regions have lower FF. The study finds a transition at log(L_Hα) ~ 37 erg s⁻¹ marking a shift from cluster-powered to single-star-ionized nebulae, and shows R_PAH anti-correlates with FF, suggesting less PAH processing in porous structures. The volumetric Hα luminosity density (L_Hα/R³) is proposed as a robust metric reducing definition-induced covariance between luminosity and radius across catalogs.
AI.motivation: Understanding the internal structure (specifically the filling factor) of H II regions is fundamental for constraining star formation processes in galaxies. The authors aim to understand how FF relates to key physical properties and whether it can serve as an evolutionary tracer through its connection with PAH emission.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 622 H II regions in NGC 628 — 475 from SIGNALS and 147 from PHANGS-MUSE. They derived luminosities, emission-line fluxes, radii, electron densities, and filling factors, and used PHANGS-JWST/MIRI imaging (7.7, 11.3, and 21 μm bands) to quantify the PAH-to-dust ratio (R_PAH). Correlations between FF, EW(Hα), luminosity, size, and R_PAH were examined, with particular attention to the L_Hα–R relation and volumetric luminosity density L_Hα/R³.
AI.result: Higher FF and EW(Hα) are found in luminous regions, while extended, low-EW(Hα) regions show lower FF. The H II region radius definition significantly affects the L_Hα–R relation. A transition is identified near log(L_Hα) ~ 37 erg s⁻¹, interpreted as the boundary between cluster-powered and single-massive-star-ionized nebulae. R_PAH correlates with L_Hα/R³, with a transition near log(L_Hα/R³) ~ 32 erg s⁻¹ corresponding to log(FF) ≈ -4.4. Lower-FF regions exhibit higher R_PAH, suggesting less efficient PAH destruction in more porous structures. These results support an evolutionary picture where FF decreases with cluster age as giant H II regions evolve toward fainter, more extended states.
AI.conclusion: The filling factor behaves as a viable evolutionary indicator for H II regions: it decreases as regions age and expand, consistent with PAH-to-dust ratio trends. The volumetric Hα luminosity density (L_Hα/R³) is a useful, robust quantity that reduces covariance between luminosity and radius induced by region-definition methods, enabling more consistent comparisons across different surveys/catalogs.

title: SPIRITS 19q: Dust Production by a Subsolar-metallicity Carbon-rich Wolf-Rayet Star in NGC 2403
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, accepted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific (PASP)
summary: We present JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of SPIRITS 19q, the highly dust-producing carbon-rich (WC) binary candidate located in a subsolar-metallicity region of the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 2403. The observations, taken in April of 2024, confirm the association of a dusty outburst observed in 2019 by the Spitzer Space Telescope with an early-type WC star. Using models from the Potsdam Wolf-Rayet (PoWR) LMC model grid we find that the WC star of SPIRITS 19q likely has an especially high mass-loss rate ($\gtrsim$ 10$^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$). From the flux peak of the IR transient as measured by Spitzer/IRAC as well as constraints on dust composition and size from the JWST spectrum, we estimate a total dust mass formed in the outburst of 6.6 $\pm$ 0.4 $\times$ 10$^{-6}$ $M_{\odot}$. Assuming a minimum orbital period of 12 years, this corresponds to a period-averaged dust production rate of $\lesssim$ 5.5 $\times$ 10$^{-7}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. These observations suggest that even a single WC system can contribute to the dust budget at subsolar metallicities, and that such systems are an important source of carbonaceous dust grains in the early universe.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of SPIRITS 19q, a dust-producing WC binary in NGC 2403, confirm the 2019 Spitzer-detected outburst originates from an early-type WC star. Spectral modeling identifies an exceptionally high mass-loss rate (~10^-4 M_sun/yr), and combined Spitzer/JWST photometric-spectroscopic constraints yield ~6.6e-6 M_sun of dust formed in the outburst. This demonstrates that single WC systems can substantially contribute to dust budgets at subsolar metallicities, relevant for carbonaceous dust in the early universe.
AI.motivation: To confirm the association between a dusty transient (SPIRITS 19q) and a WC star, characterize the WC system's properties, quantify its dust production, and assess whether such carbon-rich Wolf-Rayet systems can contribute meaningfully to dust enrichment at subsolar metallicities—relevant for understanding dust sources in the early universe.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy obtained in April 2024 was used to observe SPIRITS 19q in NGC 2403. PoWR LMC model grid fitting was used to constrain the WC star's stellar parameters and mass-loss rate. Dust mass was estimated by combining the Spitzer/IRAC flux peak of the IR transient with dust composition and size constraints derived from the JWST spectrum.
AI.result: The WC star of SPIRITS 19q has an especially high mass-loss rate of at least ~10^-4 M_sun/yr. The total dust mass formed in the outburst is 6.6 ± 0.4 × 10^-6 M_sun. With a minimum orbital period assumption of 12 years, the period-averaged dust production rate is at most ~5.5 × 10^-7 M_sun/yr.
AI.conclusion: Even a single binary WC system can significantly contribute to the dust budget at subsolar metallicities, implying WC systems are an important source of carbonaceous dust grains in the early universe.

title: Investigating the Young Stellar Populations and Hierarchies in Nearby Galaxies with the UVIT. III. Evidence for a Largest Scale of Correlated Stellar Structures and a Non-universal Fractal Dimension
comment: Submitted to the Astrophysical Journal (ApJ). Comments are welcome. 29 pages, 14 figures
summary: Scale-free turbulent motions, gravitational collapse and galactic dynamics govern galactic-scale, hierarchical organization of star formation (SF) within galaxies. Past studies suggest that properties of SF hierarchies depend upon host galaxy properties and interstellar medium (ISM) conditions. To characterize SF hierarchies, we performed two-point correlation function analysis on ~25000 UV-selected star-forming clumps (SFCs) identified in a morphologically diverse sample of 8 classic spirals, 6 flocculent spirals and 3 dwarf irregulars. We found that SF hierarchies in galaxies exhibit a maximum spatial scale -- the correlation length ($l_{\rm corr}$) -- largest scale up to which SF is spatially correlated, presumably owing to ISM turbulence. The $l_{\rm corr}$ values range from ~100 pc to 3.4 kpc and exhibit strong dependence on the galaxy's stellar mass, morphology and nature of spiral arms. This suggests that a galaxy's gravitational potential and spiral structure place an upper limit on the sizes of the largest, hierarchically structured SF complexes. Connecting $l_{\rm corr}$ with turbulence injection sources suggests that stellar feedback in dwarf irregulars, whereas disk instabilities and spiral structure in classic/flocculent spirals dominate towards sustaining their SF hierarchies up to the $l_{\rm corr}$ scale. These hierarchies disperse to near-random distributions on timescales ($T_{\rm dis}$) ranging from 20-160 Myr. The broad range of derived $l_{\rm corr}$, projected fractal dimension ($D_2$ $\in$ 0.71$-$1.73), and $T_{\rm dis}$ indicates a non-universal, galaxy-specific nature of SF hierarchies. In this work, full coverage of each galaxy's star-forming extent with the AstroSat-UltraViolet Imaging Telescope uniquely enabled us to connect global parameters of SF hierarchies with large-scale galaxy properties.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze ~25,000 UV-selected star-forming clumps across 17 galaxies of varied morphology using two-point correlation functions to find that star formation hierarchies have a maximum spatial scale (correlation length l_corr, ~100 pc to 3.4 kpc) set by the host galaxy's gravitational potential and spiral structure. The correlation length depends on stellar mass, morphology, and spiral arm nature, with stellar feedback dominating in dwarf irregulars while disk instabilities and spiral structure dominate in spirals. These hierarchies disperse over 20-160 Myr, and the broad range of derived parameters indicates non-universal, galaxy-specific star formation hierarchies.
AI.motivation: To characterize the hierarchical organization of star formation across galaxies and understand how host galaxy properties and interstellar medium conditions shape the spatial scales of star formation hierarchies.
AI.method: Two-point correlation function analysis performed on ~25,000 UV-selected star-forming clumps (SFCs) identified from a morphologically diverse sample of 8 classic spirals, 6 flocculent spirals, and 3 dwarf irregulars, using full star-forming extent coverage from the AstroSat-UltraViolet Imaging Telescope.
AI.result: SF hierarchies exhibit a maximum spatial correlation length (l_corr) ranging from ~100 pc to 3.4 kpc, strongly dependent on stellar mass, morphology, and spiral arm nature. Correlation lengths connect with turbulence injection sources (stellar feedback in dwarf irregulars; disk instabilities and spiral structure in spirals). Hierarchies disperse over timescales of 20-160 Myr, with projected fractal dimensions D2 in 0.71-1.73.
AI.conclusion: Star formation hierarchies are non-universal and galaxy-specific, with a galaxy's gravitational potential and spiral structure placing an upper limit on the sizes of the largest structured star-forming complexes. Full coverage of each galaxy's star-forming extent uniquely enabled linking global parameters of SF hierarchies with large-scale galaxy properties.

title: Discovery of the First-Ever Recorded Fading Event of the Wolf-Rayet Star WR 59
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Presents primary visual data alongside calibrated NASA TESS spaceborne overlays
summary: This paper presents the visual discovery of the first-ever recorded fading event of the Wolf-Rayet star WR 59. Historically documented as a stable star with an approximate magnitude of 13.9, the star underwent a sudden major decline during high-cadence visual monitoring in May 2021. On 11 May 2021 (JD 2459346), I observed the star plunge 1.3 magnitudes to a deep minimum of magnitude 15.2. It remained in this faded state for roughly 1 day before undergoing a structured 14-day recovery back to its baseline. This episode was independently verified by NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) during Sector 38. The satellite's calibrated data stream confirms that the timing, structure, and recovery of the fade matched the ground-based observations. While a close 11.7 V companion star masked the true depth of the drop for automated large-pixel survey pipelines, this event firmly establishes WR 59 as an active dust-producing system. It demonstrates how high-magnification visual monitoring can successfully resolve crowded stellar fields.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the visual discovery of the first-ever recorded fading event of the Wolf-Rayet star WR 59, observed on 11 May 2021 when it plunged 1.3 magnitudes for ~1 day before a 14-day recovery, independently confirmed by NASA's TESS satellite.
AI.motivation: To document and analyze the first recorded fading event of WR 59, a historically stable Wolf-Rayet star, and to validate that such events can be captured through high-cadence ground-based visual monitoring despite challenges from crowded stellar fields and nearby companions.
AI.method: High-cadence visual monitoring of WR 59 in May 2021, complemented by NASA's TESS satellite data (Sector 38) for independent verification of the timing, structure, and recovery of the fading event.
AI.result: WR 59 underwent a sudden 1.3-magnitude decline to a minimum of magnitude 15.2 on 11 May 2021, remained faded for ~1 day, then exhibited a structured 14-day recovery to baseline. TESS data confirmed the event's timing and structure. A close 11.7 magnitude companion had previously masked the true depth of the drop in automated survey pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The fading event establishes WR 59 as an active dust-producing system and demonstrates the capability of high-magnification visual monitoring to resolve crowded stellar fields and detect transient events that automated pipelines may miss.

title: The fraction of clumpy star-forming galaxies in nearby galaxies from CLAUDS and HSC-SSP
comment: Accepted 2026 September 1 by MNRAS
summary: Massive, star-forming clumps are regions of intensive star-formation that are commonly observed in high-redshift ($z > 1$) galaxies. Observations of low-redshift clumpy galaxy analogues are rare but the availability of wide-field galaxy survey data makes the detection of large clumpy galaxy samples much more feasible. We present a population of 12,790 star-forming clumps detected in a mass-complete sample of 5,395 star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at redshifts $z\leq0.32$, located in the XMM-LSS, E-COSMOS and DEEP2-3 fields observed by the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Survey (HSC-SSP) and CFHT Large Area U-band Deep Survey (CLAUDS). The clumps were detected using an improved version of our Deep Learning (DL)-based object detection framework which uses the ZOOBOT foundation DL-model as a 'backbone' feature extractor. We determined the fraction of star-forming galaxies hosting at least one off-centre clump ($f_{\mathrm{clumpy}}$) based on a clump definition that requires a clump-galaxy flux ratio in the CLAUDS u-band of $\geq8\%$. We estimate $f_{\mathrm{clumpy}}$ to decrease from $\sim$31\% at $z\sim0.3$ to $\sim$23\% at $z \sim 0.1$, which aligns well with a low-redshift extrapolation of the clumpy fraction that is measured using high-redshift observations. At fixed redshift, $f_{\mathrm{clumpy}}$ is negatively correlated with the stellar mass and positively correlated with the specific star-formation rate (sSFR) of the host galaxies. When the clump definition is changed to include only clumps with a stellar mass of $M_{\mathrm{cl}} \geq 10^7 M_\odot$, we observe a highly increased clumpy fraction of $\sim$60\% that tends to increase with the stellar mass of the host galaxies but does not show a dependence on the sSFR of the host galaxies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a population of 12,790 star-forming clumps detected in a mass-complete sample of 5,395 star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at z≤0.32 from HSC-SSP and CLAUDS surveys, using an improved deep-learning-based object detection framework built on the ZOOBOT foundation model. The clumpy galaxy fraction decreases from ~31% at z~0.3 to ~23% at z~0.1, consistent with low-redshift extrapolation from high-z observations, and correlates negatively with stellar mass and positively with sSFR. Using a stricter clump definition (M_cl≥10^7 M_sun), the clumpy fraction rises to ~60%, increases with stellar mass, and shows no sSFR dependence.
AI.motivation: Massive star-forming clumps are common in high-redshift (z>1) galaxies, but low-redshift analogues are rare. The authors aim to leverage wide-field survey data to build a large statistical sample of low-redshift clumpy galaxies, enabling characterization of clumpy fractions and their dependence on galaxy properties to connect with high-redshift observations.
AI.method: Clumps were detected in a mass-complete sample of 5,395 SFGs at z≤0.32 in the XMM-LSS, E-COSMOS, and DEEP2-3 fields using an improved deep-learning object detection framework that employs the ZOOBOT foundation model as a backbone feature extractor. Clumpy fraction f_clumpy was defined using a clump-galaxy flux ratio ≥8% in the CLAUDS u-band.
AI.result: f_clumpy decreases from ~31% at z~0.3 to ~23% at z~0.1. At fixed redshift it correlates negatively with stellar mass and positively with sSFR. With a stricter clump definition (M_cl≥10^7 M_sun), the clumpy fraction becomes ~60%, increases with stellar mass, and shows no dependence on sSFR.
AI.conclusion: The low-redshift clumpy fraction aligns well with a low-redshift extrapolation of high-redshift measurements. The clumpy fraction depends on both the adopted clump definition and host galaxy properties (stellar mass, sSFR), demonstrating that clump fraction evolution must be interpreted in the context of these dependencies.

title: The Influence of Evaporation on the Formation and Evolution of Huntsman Systems
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Huntsman systems are a recently identified and rare subclass of millisecond pulsar (MSP) binaries, characterized by a detached neutron star and an evolved giant companion in relatively wide orbits. Their formation has been proposed to involve red-bump-induced detachment, whereas the influence of MSP-driven evaporation during this evolutionary stage has not yet been quantitatively assessed. We quantify the influence of MSP-driven evaporation on the formation and evolution of Huntsman systems and assess its effects on their observable properties. We performed detailed binary evolution calculations including MSP-driven evaporation over a wide range of initial binary parameters and combined them with binary population synthesis to predict the observable population of Huntsman systems. We find that Huntsman systems originate primarily from binaries undergoing Case B mass transfer and red-bump-induced detachment, with initial donor masses of $1.0-2.5\ M_\odot$ and orbital periods above the bifurcation period. Evaporation has a secondary effect, slightly modifying the orbital evolution and the duration of the detached phase, but does not significantly alter the formation parameter space or the expected population, which contains about 10 Huntsman systems. We further show that evaporation can produce systematic shifts in the white dwarf mass-orbital period relation at the low-mass end, leading to systematically wider final orbits for a given white dwarf mass.

AI.tldr: This paper quantitatively assesses the influence of MSP-driven evaporation on the formation and evolution of Huntsman systems (rare millisecond pulsar binaries with evolved giant companions), finding that evaporation is a secondary effect that slightly modifies orbital evolution and detached-phase duration, does not significantly alter formation parameter space or population size (~10 systems), but can produce systematic shifts in the white dwarf mass-orbital period relation at the low-mass end.
AI.motivation: Huntsman systems are a recently identified, rare subclass of MSP binaries whose formation has been proposed to involve red-bump-induced detachment. However, the influence of MSP-driven evaporation during this evolutionary stage has not yet been quantitatively assessed, motivating this study.
AI.method: The authors performed detailed binary evolution calculations including MSP-driven evaporation over a wide range of initial binary parameters, combined with binary population synthesis to predict the observable population of Huntsman systems.
AI.result: Huntsman systems primarily originate from binaries undergoing Case B mass transfer and red-bump-induced detachment, with initial donor masses of 1.0-2.5 solar masses and orbital periods above the bifurcation period. Evaporation has a secondary effect, slightly modifying orbital evolution and detached-phase duration but not significantly altering the formation parameter space. The expected population contains about 10 Huntsman systems. Evaporation can produce systematic shifts in the white dwarf mass-orbital period relation at the low-mass end, leading to systematically wider final orbits for a given white dwarf mass.
AI.conclusion: MSP-driven evaporation does not significantly affect the formation or population of Huntsman systems, but it can systematically shift the white dwarf mass-orbital period relation at the low-mass end, producing wider final orbits. This provides an additional constraint for comparing theoretical models with observed Huntsman systems.

title: Sulphur within the extreme environment of the central molecular zone of NGC 253: a chemical modelling approach
comment: 19 pages, 18 figures; To be published in A&A
summary: Sulphur(S)-bearing species are ubiquitous in Galactic star-forming regions, from dense cold cores to outflows and shocks linked to protostellar activity. A recent observational study investigated the origin of S-bearing species towards the central molecular zone (CMZ) of NGC 253 and showed that Sulphur emission is linked to the presence of forming stars. However, more extensive modelling of these observations are required to determine the exact origin of the Sulphur emission (e.g. shock or thermal evaporation). Using chemical modelling, we examine how S-bearing species behave in the more extreme environment of the starburst galaxy NGC 253, and more generally, how they can help us improve our understanding of the emission linked with the dense star-forming gas in external galaxies. We use the gas-grain time-dependent chemical model UCLCHEM to model static warm clouds and C-type shocks under the physical conditions found in the CMZ of NGC 253. We compare observed abundances and abundance ratios to the modelled output abundances. We found that depending on the model type (shock, post-shock or static cloud), the highest abundance reached by the S-bearing species varies significantly. Hence, we can use their observed abundances of S-bearing species to distinguish between shocked, post-shocked or a quiescent (non-shocked) gas. We also confirm observationally-based conclusions on their emission origins, including in the case of unresolved emission. Comparing GMC-scale observations with chemical modelling is a powerful method to investigate and constrain the origin of molecular emission towards extragalactic star-forming regions. Sulphur-bearing species are useful to distinguish between different types of ISM components (shocked/post-shocked/quiescent gas).

AI.tldr: This paper uses the gas-grain chemical model UCLCHEM to model S-bearing species in static warm clouds and C-type shocks under conditions found in the central molecular zone of the starburst galaxy NGC 253. By comparing modeled abundances to observations, the authors show that S-bearing species can be used to distinguish between shocked, post-shocked, and quiescent gas components in extragalactic star-forming regions.
AI.motivation: Observations of S-bearing species towards the CMZ of NGC 253 linked sulphur emission to forming stars, but the exact origin of the emission (shock vs. thermal evaporation) remains unclear. More extensive chemical modeling is required to determine the physical origin of the observed sulphur emission.
AI.method: The authors employ the gas-grain time-dependent chemical model UCLCHEM to simulate static warm clouds and C-type shocks under physical conditions representative of the CMZ of NGC 253. They then compare observed column densities/abundances and abundance ratios of S-bearing species to the model output.
AI.result: The peak abundances of S-bearing species differ significantly depending on model type (shock, post-shock, or static cloud). This allows observed abundances of S-bearing species to be used as discriminators between shocked, post-shocked, and quiescent gas. Observational conclusions on emission origins are confirmed, including for unresolved emission.
AI.conclusion: Comparing GMC-scale observations with chemical modelling is a powerful approach for constraining the origin of molecular emission in extragalactic star-forming regions. S-bearing species serve as effective tracers to distinguish between different types of ISM components (shocked/post-shocked/quiescent gas).

title: On the photospheric abundances of the B-type fast rotator Regulus
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables; 4 files as online material; submitted to PASJ
summary: A spectroscopic study of Regulus (late B-type rapidly-rotating star) was conducted with an aim of investigating its photospheric chemical abundances (especially for light elements), which has barely been challenged so far because of the considerable difficulty of abundance determination for such a very fast rotator (>~300 km/s). The atmospheric parameters were determined to be T_eff = 12345K (effective temperature) and log g = 3.58 (surface gravity) based on the spectral energy distribution, while the microturbulence was estimated as v_t = 0.5 km/s. The abundances of 14 elements (He, C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, S, Ca, Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, and Ni) were derived by applying the spectrum-fitting technique, where the non-LTE effect was taken into account for lighter elements from He to Ca. The resulting relative-to-the-Sun abundances ([X/H]) revealed a remarkable trend that, while most elements indicate near-solar abundances (within +/-<~0.3dex), only C shows a marked deficiency ([C/H]~ -1.4) which is hard to explain. For example, a simple scenario of C underabundance caused by mixing of CN-cycled product (e.g., due to rapid rotation or binary mass transfer) is unlikely because any N enrichment is not observed. This problem remains yet to be further investigated.

AI.tldr: A spectroscopic analysis of the rapidly rotating late B-type star Regulus determined its atmospheric parameters (T_eff=12345K, log g=3.58, v_t=0.5 km/s) and derived photospheric abundances for 14 elements using spectrum-fitting with non-LTE corrections for lighter elements. While most elements show near-solar abundances, carbon exhibits a striking deficiency of ~1.4 dex that cannot be explained by simple CN-cycling mixing scenarios due to the absence of corresponding nitrogen enrichment.
AI.motivation: Chemical abundance determination for Regulus, a very fast rotator (>~300 km/s), has barely been attempted due to the considerable difficulty of abundance analysis in such rotationally broadened spectra. This study aims to fill this gap, particularly focusing on light element abundances.
AI.method: Atmospheric parameters (T_eff and log g) were determined from the spectral energy distribution; microturbulence was estimated. Abundances of 14 elements (He through Ni) were derived via a spectrum-fitting technique, with non-LTE corrections applied to lighter elements from He to Ca.
AI.result: Most elements show near-solar abundances within ±<~0.3 dex, but carbon displays a marked deficiency of [C/H] ~ -1.4, which is difficult to explain. The expected nitrogen enrichment accompanying carbon depletion from CN-cycled product mixing (via rapid rotation or binary mass transfer) is not observed.
AI.conclusion: The unexplained carbon underabundance in Regulus (without corresponding N enrichment) remains an open problem requiring further investigation.

title: The Physical Conditions of Low-Mass Galaxies at z=3.5-7.0 from JWST Spectroscopy: The Behaviour of Spectral Line Ratios with Burstiness
comment: 28 pages, including 1 appendix and 16 figures. Submitted to the ApJ, comments welcome
summary: We present a study of the physical conditions of galaxies at redshifts $z=3.5-7.0$, based on emission-line diagnostics of JWST NIRSpec spectra for 1889 star-forming sources spanning more than 4~dex in stellar mass. We find that the median H$α$/H$β$ and [OIII]/H$β$ are constant throughout these redshifts, indicating a slow evolution of the interstellar medium conditions from the Epoch of Reionization to Cosmic Noon. The stellar-mass evolution of these line ratios follow the expected trend for chemical enrichment and dust build-up, with \ohb~being maximum for galaxies with $\rm M_{\star} \approx 10^9 \, \rm M_\odot$, and the medians of H$α$/H$β$ and [OII]/H$β$ monotonically increasing from $\rm{M}_{\rm \star} \approx 10^7$ through $ \approx 10^{10}\, \rm M_\odot$. Focusing on the 1552 low stellar-mass ($<10^9 \, \rm M_\odot$) galaxies, we particularly investigate the behaviour of the main spectral-line ratios with burstiness. We find a significantly higher degree of scatter in [OIII]/H$β$ and [OII]/H$β$ for high-burstiness than for low-burstiness galaxies. Values of log([OIII]/H$β$)~$\gtrsim 0.8$ are almost exclusively seen amongst those with high burstiness. Meanwhile, log([OIII]/H$β$)~$\lesssim 0.3$ are virtually not found amongst high-burstiness galaxies, except at the lowest stellar masses $\mathrm{log(M_\star/M_\odot)}<7.5$. Our results are consistent with a scenario in which star-formation bursts produce temporary chemical enrichment that is quickly lost via stellar winds. They also suggest that metallicity measures in bursting galaxies are unstable, and that the search for the most metal-poor objects should optimally be conducted amongst low-burstiness or very low-stellar mass sources.

AI.tldr: Study of physical conditions of galaxies at z=3.5-7.0 using JWST NIRSpec emission-line diagnostics for 1889 star-forming galaxies spanning >4 dex in stellar mass. Median Hα/Hβ and [OIII]/Hβ remain constant across these redshifts, indicating slow ISM evolution from reionization to cosmic noon. Line ratio trends with stellar mass follow chemical enrichment/dust buildup expectations. Among low-mass galaxies, high-burstiness sources show greater scatter in [OIII]/Hβ and [OII]/Hβ, consistent with transient chemical enrichment from star-formation bursts that is quickly lost via stellar winds.
AI.motivation: To characterize the evolution of interstellar medium conditions (gas metallicity, dust, ionization) in galaxies from the Epoch of Reionization (z~7) to Cosmic Noon (z~3.5), and understand how star-formation burstiness affects chemical enrichment patterns, particularly in low-mass galaxies.
AI.method: Using emission-line diagnostics from JWST NIRSpec spectra of 1889 star-forming galaxies at z=3.5-7.0 spanning >4 dex in stellar mass. Line ratios Hα/Hβ, [OIII]/Hβ, and [OII]/Hβ are analyzed as functions of redshift and stellar mass. The sample includes 1552 low stellar-mass (<10^9 Msun) galaxies, for which scatter in line ratios is examined as a function of galaxy burstiness.
AI.result: Median Hα/Hβ and [OIII]/Hβ are constant across z=3.5-7.0. Line ratios evolve with stellar mass following chemical enrichment expectations, with [OIII]/Hβ peaking near M*≈10^9 Msun and Hα/Hβ and [OII]/Hβ increasing monotonically from ~10^7 to ~10^10 Msun. High-burstiness galaxies show significantly larger scatter in [OIII]/Hβ and [OII]/Hβ. Extreme high values of log([OIII]/Hβ)≳0.8 occur almost exclusively in high-burstiness galaxies, while log([OIII]/Hβ)≲0.3 are essentially absent among high-burstiness systems except at very low stellar masses (<10^7.5 Msun).
AI.conclusion: The results support a scenario where star-formation bursts cause temporary chemical enrichment that is rapidly lost via stellar winds. Metallicity estimates in bursting galaxies are unstable; therefore searches for the most metal-poor galaxies should target low-burstiness or very low-stellar-mass systems.

title: Kinematic Relationship Between Solar Extreme Ultraviolet Waves and Type II Metric Radio Bursts
comment: 13 pages, 06 figures, 01 table (accepted for publication in Scientific Reports)
summary: Solar extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) waves are large-scale disturbances that manifest as bright wavefronts, often during coronal mass ejections (CMEs). According to the magnetic field line stretching model, this phenomenon comprises two components: a fast-mode CME piston-driven shock wave and a slower, nonwave component. They are often associated with solar type II radio bursts. It is expected the radio source and the fast-mode EUV wave should come from different parts of the same shock, i.e., the CME piston-driven shock, and their speeds should be strongly correlated. To investigate this relationship, we utilized high spatiotemporal resolution observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory in conjunction with radio data from the Radio Solar Telescope Network. Our analysis reveals that there exists a linear correlation between the EUV fast-mode speeds ($v_{euv}$) and the shock speeds derived from metric (m) type II radio bursts ($v_{radio}$), which is $v_{radio}=0.89v_{euv}+51$ kms$^{-1}$, with a correlation coefficient of 0.77. This strong correlation suggests that original coronal EIT waves, which are about three times slower than type II radio bursts, are not fast-mode waves, and it is misleading to map type II radio bursts to EIT waves in the literature.

AI.tldr: The study investigates the relationship between fast-mode EUV waves and type II radio bursts using SDO and RSTN observations, finding a strong linear correlation ($v_{radio}=0.89v_{euv}+51$ km/s, r=0.77), which suggests EUV fast-mode waves and type II radio sources originate from the same CME-driven shock, while original EIT waves are not fast-mode waves.
AI.motivation: To investigate the relationship between fast-mode EUV waves and type II radio burst shock speeds, testing whether they originate from different parts of the same CME piston-driven shock, and to clarify whether EIT waves commonly mapped to type II bursts in the literature are actually fast-mode waves.
AI.method: Utilized high spatiotemporal resolution observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) alongside radio data from the Radio Solar Telescope Network (RSTN). Measured EUV fast-mode wave speeds ($v_{euv}$) and compared them with shock speeds derived from metric type II radio bursts ($v_{radio}$) through correlation analysis.
AI.result: Found a linear relationship between EUV fast-mode speeds and type II radio burst shock speeds: $v_{radio}=0.89v_{euv}+51$ kms$^{-1}$, with a correlation coefficient of 0.77, indicating a strong correlation between the two quantities.
AI.conclusion: The strong correlation confirms that EUV fast-mode waves and type II radio bursts originate from the same CME piston-driven shock. Since original coronal EIT waves are approximately three times slower than type II radio bursts, they are not fast-mode waves, and mapping type II radio bursts to EIT waves in the literature is misleading.

title: Slow stellar halo rotation as a signature of disc flips and GES-like mergers
comment: 12 pages, 11 figures, accepted to MNRAS
summary: The stellar halo of the Milky Way (MW) exhibits a weak net prograde rotational signal ($v_φ \lesssim 25$ km~s$^{-1}$), yet its origin remains unexplained. To investigate this, we use the Auriga cosmological simulation suite of MW-mass haloes to probe the rotation of stellar haloes over the redshift range $z_{\mathrm{red}}=0-2.5$. The rotational signal is found to persist over this redshift range. We show that satellite progenitors of the stellar halo exhibit a non-uniform distribution of infall directions, with a tendency to align with the host disc, albeit with significant scatter. Thus, we attribute the net rotation to the anisotropic accretion of satellites. Haloes that host \textit{Gaia}-Enceladus-Sausage (GES)-like substructures exhibit consistently slower rotational velocity, likely due to the head-on, more radial trajectory of the dominant progenitor in such systems. Haloes whose stellar discs have reorientated by $\geq 90^{\circ}$ also exhibit slower rotation, likely because the longer dynamical timescales of haloes prevent them from quickly adjusting to disc reorientations. We also report a correlation between the rotation of stellar and dark matter haloes, suggesting a possible common origin driven by anisotropic accretion. We therefore suggest that the MW experienced a disc flip and has a slowly rotating dark matter halo.

AI.tldr: Using the Auriga cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass haloes from z=0-2.5, this paper shows that the weak net prograde rotation of stellar haloes (v_phi ≤ 25 km/s) persists across cosmic time and attributes it to anisotropic satellite accretion. Haloes with Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage-like substructures or those that experienced stellar disc reorientation ≥90° rotate more slowly. A correlation between stellar and dark matter halo rotation suggests a common origin via anisotropic accretion, implying the MW experienced a disc flip and has a slowly rotating dark matter halo.
AI.motivation: The origin of the Milky Way stellar halo's weak net prograde rotation remains unexplained; this paper aims to identify the physical mechanism driving this rotation using cosmological simulations.
AI.method: Analysis of the Auriga cosmological simulation suite of MW-mass haloes, probing the rotational signal of stellar haloes over redshift z=0-2.5, examining satellite infall directions, GES-like substructures, disc reorientation events, and the correlation between stellar and dark matter halo rotation.
AI.result: The net prograde rotation persists across z=0-2.5. Satellite progenitors show anisotropic infall aligned (with scatter) with the host disc, explaining the net rotation. GES-like haloes and haloes with ≥90° disc reorientation exhibit slower rotation. Stellar and dark matter halo rotations are correlated, suggesting a shared anisotropic accretion origin.
AI.conclusion: The MW's stellar halo rotation arises from anisotropic satellite accretion. The findings imply the MW experienced a disc flip and possesses a slowly rotating dark matter halo.

title: X-shooter survey Across Regions and Ages to probe Disk Evolution (ARADE): Accretion properties in Orion A and their relation with disk masses
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 20 pages, 9 figures (including appendix)
summary: We present a homogeneous VLT/X-Shooter study of accretion in young stellar objects spanning the entire Orion A complex. Our sample includes 91 pre-main-sequence stars hosting a protoplanetary disk according to Spitzer photometry, of which 34 have complementary ALMA dust mass measurements. We derived stellar and accretion properties using a self-consistent multi-component fitting procedure. Our sample encompasses spectral types from K3 down to M5, corresponding to stellar masses within $\sim$0.8-0.1 $M_{\odot}$. The accretion-stellar luminosity ($L_{acc}-L_{\star}$) and the mass accretion rate-stellar mass ($\dot{M}_{acc}-M_{\star}$) scaling relations in Orion A are consistent with those of other star-forming regions (SFRs) that span a range of stellar densities, far-ultraviolet (FUV) irradiation fields, and ages, with all regions occupying the same locus in parameter space. For the 34 sources with complementary dust mass measurements, we present the first investigation of the $\dot{M}_{acc}$ and disk mass ($M_{disk}$) correlation in Orion A, recovering a spread consistent with that reported for other regions. Despite our sample spanning nearly five orders of magnitude in local FUV field strength, we find no statistically significant correlation between $\dot{M}_{acc}$ and FUV irradiation. However, by combining our sample with literature measurements in Lupus, the Orion Nebula Cluster, and $σ$ Orionis, we find a tentative population-level decrease of the inferred disk lifetime $t_{\rm disk} =M_{disk}/\dot{M}_{acc}$ toward stronger FUV environments, though large intrinsic scatter and limited sample sizes at intermediate and high FUV fields prevent firm conclusions. The homogeneous $\dot{M}_{acc}$ measurements reported here provide a solid foundation for future studies of accretion and disk evolution across the diverse environments of Orion A and other SFRs.

AI.tldr: A homogeneous VLT/X-Shooter survey of 91 young stellar objects across the Orion A complex provides accretion properties for stars spanning K3 to M5 spectral types. The accretion–luminosity and accretion rate–mass scaling relations match those of other star-forming regions. Combining their sample with literature data from other regions, the authors find tentative evidence that disk lifetimes decrease in stronger FUV environments, though scatter limits firm conclusions.
AI.motivation: To characterize stellar accretion and disk properties homogeneously across the environmentally diverse Orion A complex, and to test whether accretion rates and disk evolution are influenced by environmental factors such as stellar density, FUV irradiation, and age.
AI.method: VLT/X-Shooter spectroscopy of 91 pre-main-sequence stars (selected via Spitzer protoplanetary disk detections, 34 with ALMA dust mass measurements). Stellar and accretion parameters derived via a self-consistent multi-component fitting procedure. Scaling relations examined and compared to other star-forming regions; disk lifetime was computed as M_disk/Mdot and analyzed against FUV field strength.
AI.result: The L_acc–L_star and Mdot–M_star relations in Orion A are consistent with those of other regions. No significant correlation is found between mass accretion rate and FUV irradiation within the sample, spanning ~5 orders of magnitude in FUV field. A tentative population-level decrease in disk lifetime is seen toward stronger FUV fields when combined with literature samples from Lupus, ONC, and sigma Orionis, though large scatter and small samples limit certainty.
AI.conclusion: Accretion properties in Orion A follow universal scaling relations shared across diverse star-forming regions. Environmental effects on disk dispersal remain inconclusive at the individual level, but a population-level trend of shortened disk lifetimes in high-FUV environments may exist. The homogeneous accretion measurements provide a foundation for future comparative disk evolution studies.

title: Collisional excitation of cyclopentadiene by helium. A complete set of rate coefficients and astrophysical applications
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures
summary: Complex organic molecules, including large cyclic species, are prevalent in interstellar space and play a key role in various astrochemical processes. Cyclopentadiene (c-C5H6) is a five-membered cyclic hydrocarbon recently detected in TMC-1 and some other interstellar molecular clouds. While accurate spectroscopic data were available, collisional rate coefficients for its rotational transitions were missing so far, introducing a potential limitation in the interpretation of the observations. This study aims to provide a comprehensive set of state-to-state thermal rate coefficients for the rotational excitation of c-C5H6 due to collisions with helium, crucial for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer modelling in astrophysical environments, and to examine how far the molecule is from thermalisation under the physical conditions of cold molecular clouds. The research employed accurate quantum scattering calculations using the close-coupling (CC) and coupled states (CS) methods, based on a highly-correlated three-dimensional potential energy surface for the [c-C5H6 + He] collisional complex. Calculations were performed for a wide range of rotational states (from j = 0 to j \leq 25) and kinetic temperatures (from 10 to 50 K). We calculated a complete set of thermal rate coefficients for both ortho- and para-C5H6. Radiative transfer simulations demonstrated that most rotational levels of cyclopentadiene are fully thermalized under typical cold cloud conditions and exhibit minor non-LTE effects. Nevertheless, this study is the first to utilise accurate state-to-state rate coefficients for radiative transfer simulation of a large, five-membered cyclic species detected in space. This allows to draw some general conclusions and paves the way for future studies of complex astromolecules that will enable a more precise interpretation of upcoming detections.

AI.tldr: This study provides the first comprehensive set of state-to-state thermal rate coefficients for rotational excitation of cyclopentadiene (c-C5H6) by helium collisions, using accurate quantum scattering calculations (CC and CS methods) on a highly-correlated 3D PES, covering rotational states up to j≤25 and temperatures 10-50 K for both ortho- and para-C5H6. Radiative transfer simulations show most rotational levels are thermalized under cold molecular cloud conditions, with only minor non-LTE effects.
AI.motivation: Cyclopentadiene (c-C5H6), a cyclic molecule recently detected in TMC-1 and other interstellar clouds, lacked collisional rate coefficients for its rotational transitions. This missing data limited the interpretation of observations through non-LTE radiative transfer modelling, motivating the need for accurate collisional data to properly assess the molecule's excitation state in astrophysical environments.
AI.method: The research employed accurate quantum scattering calculations using the close-coupling (CC) and coupled states (CS) methods, grounded in a highly-correlated three-dimensional potential energy surface for the [c-C5H6 + He] system. Thermal rate coefficients were computed for rotational states from j=0 to j≤25 and kinetic temperatures from 10 to 50 K, for both ortho- and para-C5H6, followed by radiative transfer simulations to assess thermalisation.
AI.result: A complete set of thermal state-to-state rate coefficients was obtained for both spin isomers of cyclopentadiene. Radiative transfer simulations demonstrated that most rotational levels of c-C5H6 are fully thermalized under typical cold cloud conditions, with only minor non-LTE effects observed.
AI.conclusion: This study represents the first use of accurate state-to-state rate coefficients for radiative transfer simulation of a large, five-membered cyclic species detected in space. The findings enable general conclusions about cyclic molecule excitation and establish a framework for future studies of complex astromolecules, facilitating more precise interpretation of upcoming astronomical detections.

title: Revisiting candidates for non-pulsating stars located in the Cepheid instability strip in the Large Magellanic Cloud
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We analyzed photometric and spectroscopic data for 11 candidates for non-pulsating stars located in the Cepheid instability strip (IS) of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) in order to investigate the reasons for the lack of pulsations. We used available temperature calibrations based on photometric colors to estimate the effective temperatures of the candidates, which served as initial parameters for the spectroscopic analysis. We also applied surface brightness-color relations calibrated for Cepheid variables, giants, and supergiants to estimate stellar radii. The spectral analysis was performed using the spectral synthesis method to determine the atmospheric parameters; namely, the effective temperature, metallicity, surface gravity, microturbulent velocity, projected rotational velocity, and chemical abundances for up to ~30 elements. For most objects, only a single spectrum was available. However, no significant variations in radial velocities were detected among the stars with repeat observations; therefore, all stars were treated as single object in the analysis. Two stars exhibit broad spectral lines, which may indicate high rotational velocities or possible binarity; however, additional spectra are required to confirm this interpretation. One of these objects also shows asymmetric line profiles, which might be related to the presence of non-radial pulsation modes causing line-shape variations. A common feature among all analyzed candidates is an enhancement of barium-peak s-process elements compared to solar values. This may indicate past mass transfer from a companion during its post-asymptotic giant branch phase. This study provides an insight into the physical parameters of candidates for non-pulsating stars residing within the Cepheid IS in the LMC, although the lack of pulsations remains a mystery and challenges pulsation theory.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze photometric and spectroscopic data for 11 non-pulsating star candidates inside the Cepheid instability strip of the Large Magellanic Cloud to understand why they do not pulsate. Using temperature calibrations, surface brightness-color relations, and spectral synthesis, they determine atmospheric parameters (Teff, metallicity, log g, microturbulence, v sin i) and chemical abundances for ~30 elements. A common barium-peak s-process element enhancement suggests past mass transfer from a post-AGB companion. Despite detailed characterization, the absence of pulsations remains unresolved.
AI.motivation: To investigate why certain stars residing within the Cepheid instability strip of the LMC do not exhibit pulsations, which challenges current pulsation theory.
AI.method: Photometric color-based temperature calibrations for initial Teff estimates; surface brightness-color relations for stellar radius determination; spectral synthesis analysis to derive atmospheric parameters including effective temperature, metallicity, surface gravity, microturbulent velocity, projected rotational velocity, and chemical abundances of ~30 elements; radial velocity monitoring for variability checks.

Two objects show broad spectral lines suggesting high rotation or binarity, one with asymmetric line profiles possibly indicating non-radial pulsation modes. All candidates show enhancement of barium-peak s-process elements relative to solar values, suggesting past mass transfer from a post-asymptotic giant branch companion.
AI.conclusion: The study provides detailed physical parameters for non-pulsating Cepheid IS candidates in the LMC, but the lack of pulsations remains unexplained and continues to challenge pulsation theory.

title: Semiresolved Stellar Populations as Distance Indicators
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJL
summary: Galaxy distances are central to our understanding of the Universe. Despite the success of existing approaches, independent and complementary methods remain valuable for testing systematic effects and extending the applicability range of different distance metrics. Here we demonstrate that the spectrum of an individual semi-resolved stellar population encodes direct information about its distance and that valuable distance constraints can, in principle, be obtained by combining multiple independent measurements. When applied to optical spectra of bulge of the Andromeda galaxy (M\,31), we derive a stellar population-based distance of 756$\pm$57 kpc ($μ_0 = 24.39 \pm 0.15$), in agreement with state-of-the-art measurements. Crucially, semi-resolved stellar population distances does not require secondary calibrations, although its absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted stellar population models. Our findings provide a first assessment of the feasibility of deriving stellar population-based distance estimates from simple stellar population models, motivating further tests of the broader applicability and precision of the method.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the spectrum of a semi-resolved stellar population directly encodes distance information, and derives a distance of 756±57 kpc to M31's bulge from optical spectra using stellar population models, confirming the method's feasibility without secondary calibrations.
AI.motivation: Galaxy distances are fundamental to cosmological understanding. While existing distance methods are successful, independent and complementary approaches are needed to test systematic effects and extend the applicability of distance metrics across different regimes.
AI.method: The authors use the spectrum of an individual semi-resolved stellar population, which encodes direct distance information, and combine multiple independent measurements to extract distance constraints. The method is applied to optical spectra of the M31 bulge, using simple stellar population models.
AI.result: The stellar population-based distance to M31's bulge is derived as 756±57 kpc (μ₀ = 24.39 ± 0.15), fully consistent with state-of-the-art measurements. The method does not require secondary calibrations, though its absolute scale depends on the adopted stellar population models.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first assessment of stellar population-based distance estimation feasibility from simple stellar population models and motivates further testing of the method's broader applicability and precision.

title: Fundamental effective temperature measurements for eclipsing binary stars - IX. Characterisation of 5 solar-type sclipsing binaries with M-dwarf companions
comment: 17 pages, 13 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Large-scale spectroscopic surveys will need suitable benchmark stars that can be used to verify the performance of automatic pipelines. A promising type of object for this purpose is the detached eclipsing binary (DEB) containing an FG-star and a low temperature companion. For flux ratios $\lesssim1$~per~cent, the spectra obtained for the binary will be almost identical to a single star. As the methods for obtaining accurate parameters for binaries are well established, they would be excellent benchmark candidates. We analyse a group of DEBs with M-dwarf companions using TESS light curves and high resolution spectroscopy from NIRPS and HARPS on the ESO 3.6-m telescope. We obtain accurate fundamental parameters for the stellar components. The secondary component is visible with cross-correlation, allowing them to be characterised as well. With the stellar parameters obtained from the analysis, we can measure precise effective temperatures from Gaia parallaxes and archival magnitude data. Chemical compositions of the primary stars are also extracted from the stellar spectra. In this analysis, the secondary components have minimal impact on determined spectroscopic parameters. Our radii and masses are characterised to within sub per~cent precision as well as our primary effective temperatures. Beyond a new set of stellar benchmarks, the secondary components analysed in this work represent a well characterised sample of M-dwarf stars which will be useful to improve our understanding of low mass structure and evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes detached eclipsing binaries (DEBs) with FG-star primaries and M-dwarf companions, using TESS light curves and high-resolution spectroscopy from NIRPS/HARPS, to produce precisely characterized benchmark stars and a well-characterized sample of M-dwarfs.
AI.motivation: Large-scale spectroscopic surveys require reliable benchmark stars to verify the performance of automatic pipelines. DEBs with an FG-star and a low-temperature companion are ideal candidates because their spectra are nearly identical to single stars when flux ratios are low, yet their binary parameters can be derived with high precision using well-established methods.
AI.method: The authors combine TESS light curves with high-resolution spectroscopy (NIRPS and HARPS on the ESO 3.6-m telescope) to analyze a group of DEBs with M-dwarf companions. Stellar parameters are derived from the binary analysis; the secondary stars are visible via cross-correlation and characterized. Effective temperatures are measured from Gaia parallaxes and archival photometry, and chemical abundances of the primaries are extracted from the spectra.
AI.result: Radii, masses, and primary effective temperatures are characterized to sub-percent precision. The secondary components have minimal impact on the determined spectroscopic parameters, confirming their suitability as benchmark stars. The secondary M-dwarf components form a well-characterized sample for low-mass stellar studies.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a new set of stellar benchmark candidates suitable for pipeline validation in large-scale surveys, while the characterized M-dwarf secondary components will contribute to improved understanding of low-mass stellar structure and evolution.

title: The MWA Interestingly Deep AStrophysical (MIDAS) Survey: Survey Description and First Data Release
comment: Accepted for publication in PASA. The deep field mosaics, RMS maps, PSF maps and catalogues are available for download from: https://doi.org/10.57891/z19a-2n41
summary: We present the deepest MWA survey to date, targeting the GAMA9 and GAMA23 survey fields at 215.68 MHz. With a bandwidth of 30.72 MHz, the two images cover ${\sim}1250\text{ deg}^2$ for the GAMA9 field and ${\sim}850\text{ deg}^2$ for the GAMA23 field, with an angular resolution of ${\sim}60''$. The GAMA9 image was formed from 1 282 2-min snapshot observations (42.7 hours) and the GAMA23 image from 1 701 observations (56.7 hours) achieving depths of $0.923 \pm 0.003$ and $0.331 \pm 0.001$ mJy/beam at the field centres respectively. We processed the data with an updated version of the GLEAM-X pipeline tuned for deep surveys and make this MWA Deep Imaging Pipeline code public. Updates to the pipeline include automation of the observation downloading, calibration, and imaging along with optimisation of the CLEANing methods and parameters. Above $5σ$, we catalogue 53 419 and 80 407 radio components in the GAMA9 and GAMA23 fields respectively. We find that the completeness corrected source counts for both fields are in good agreement down to $25$-$50$ mJy with those from LOFAR and earlier MWA surveys. We demonstrate the utility of this survey by highlighting a few sources of particular interest and describing future science possible with this survey.

AI.tldr: A deep Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) radio survey at 215.68 MHz covering GAMA9 and GAMA23 fields (~1250 and ~850 deg²), with ~60'' resolution, reaching depths of 0.923 and 0.331 mJy/beam respectively. They release an updated GLEAM-X pipeline (MWA Deep Imaging Pipeline) and catalogue 53,419 and 80,407 radio components above 5σ in the two fields, with source counts consistent with LOFAR and earlier MWA surveys down to 25–50 mJy.
AI.motivation: To produce the deepest MWA survey to date in the GAMA fields and provide a public, automated deep-imaging pipeline, enabling deeper low-frequency radio source characterisation and supporting future multi-wavelength and transient/evolutionary science.
AI.method: The survey combines many 2-minute MWA snapshot observations (1,282 in GAMA9 and 1,701 in GAMA23) into wide, deep images at 215.68 MHz with 30.72 MHz bandwidth and ~60'' resolution. An updated/automated GLEAM-X pipeline (new public "MWA Deep Imaging Pipeline") handles observation downloading, calibration, and imaging, with optimised CLEANing methods. Source counts are completeness corrected and compared with LOFAR and earlier MWA surveys.
AI.result: Images reach depths of 0.923±0.003 mJy/beam (GAMA9) and 0.331±0.001 mJy/beam (GAMA23). 53,419 and 80,407 radio components are catalogued above 5σ in GAMA9 and GAMA23 respectively. Completeness-corrected source counts agree well with LOFAR and earlier MWA results down to 25–50 mJy.
AI.conclusion: The deepest MWA survey in these fields validates the upgraded pipeline and demonstrates good consistency with existing low-frequency surveys. It showcases a selection of notable sources and indicates future scientific applications, providing a useful public dataset and pipeline for the community.

title: Archival transients detected with the MeerLICHT telescope I: Supernovae
summary: Wide-field optical transient surveys collectively discover $\sim$50 new transients per night, making rapid, multi-filter and/or spectroscopic follow-up of all but the most exceptional events unfeasible. Consequently, the (early) light-curve properties of most supernovae (SNe), particularly sub-luminous events, are often poorly characterised. Here, we showcase recovery of key parameters by combining publicly available data from multiple, contemporaneous surveys. We built a catalogue of $125$ SNe by cross-matching the MeerLICHT (ML) transient survey with the Transient Name Server list of spectroscopically classified SNe detected between August 2017 and October 2022. For a subset of $14$ SNe with good multi-survey photometric coverage, we combined ML-$q$, ZTF-$g,r$, and ATLAS-$c,o$ data to construct composite early-time light curves. We then applied an expanding fireball ($t^2$) model to constrain their explosion dates and rest-frame rise times. We find that this simple model provides a reliable description for the early emission of most SNe in our sample and successfully constrains their rise time, a key parameter for characterising SN categories and probing progenitor origins. This multi-survey approach, only using standard survey products, provides a powerful method to characterise large numbers of SNe that would otherwise be lost, a technique that will be essential for maximising the scientific return from current and future surveys such as GOTO, BlackGEM, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST, and Global Open Transient Telescope Array (GOTTA).

Applying an expanding fireball (t²) model, they constrain explosion dates and rest-frame rise times, demonstrating that this simple model reliably characterizes early SN emission using only publicly available multi-survey data.

As a result, early light-curve properties of most supernovae—particularly sub-luminous events—are poorly characterized. The authors aim to recover key SN parameters by combining publicly available data from multiple contemporaneous surveys without requiring dedicated follow-up resources.

They applied an expanding fireball (t²) model to fit these light curves and constrain explosion dates and rest-frame rise times.
